 Counted Out Before Election Day, Blue Dogs Return With Ranks More Than Doubled
 November 13, 2026 
 by Dan McCue 
 New Blue Dogs in the House! (From left to right) Johnny Garcia, Henry Cuellar, Sanford Bishop, JoAnna Mendoza, Vicente Gonzalez, Josh Gottheimer, Marie Gluesenkamp Perez > top of car > Eileen Laubacher, Bobby Pulido, Paul Barringer, Jamie Ager, Sam Forstag, > ground level> Becca Cooke, Mike Thompson, Jake Johnson, Zach Dembo, Mitchell Berman, Nancy Lacore, Bob Brooks, Jim Costa, and Zack Mullock. 
 WASHINGTON — They posed in front of the Capitol dome on a bright fall morning this week, gathered around a 1997 Toyota Land Cruiser belonging to the coalition’s chair, Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington. 
 A few sat on the roof, and at least two wore cowboy hats.
 It was the first class photo of an expanded Blue Dog Coalition, a group that just two weeks earlier had been written off as a fading force in Democratic politics.
 Just before the Nov. 3 midterms, a report in Drop Site News found the coalition down to 10 members, three of them in competitive races, with one, Rep. Jared Golden, D-Maine, retiring. 
 The report argued that the Blue Dogs, once called “majority makers” by former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., for winning Republican-leaning seats in 2006, 2008 and 2018, had become “a non-factor in the midterm spending frenzy.”
 The Midterm election results last week changed that picture. 
 On Wednesday, the Blue Dog PAC announced that it had helped elect 14 new Blue Dogs to Congress. It said the coalition will have 23 members when the 120th Congress convenes in January, which would more than double its size.
 Katie Phillips, the PAC’s executive director, said every returning member of the coalition is rejoining, along with every PAC-endorsed candidate who won.
 “From Texas and North Carolina to Montana, Wisconsin, and South Carolina, Blue Dog candidates won in communities where Democrats have struggled to compete for years,” the PAC said. It called the cycle one of the most successful in the coalition’s 30-year history.
 The new class includes Reps.-elect Johnny Garcia and Bobby Pulido of Texas, JoAnna Mendoza of Arizona, Jamie Ager and Paul Barringer of North Carolina, Sam Forstag of Montana, Rebecca Cooke and Mitchell Berman of Wisconsin, Jake Johnson of Minnesota, Zach Dembo of Kentucky, Nancy Lacore of South Carolina, Bob Brooks of Pennsylvania, Zack Mullock of New Jersey and Eileen Laubacher of Colorado.
 Several of them unseated Republican incumbents. 
 Barringer defeated Rep. Brad Knott in North Carolina’s 13th District, and Mullock beat Rep. Jeff Van Drew in New Jersey’s 2nd. Laubacher, a retired Navy rear admiral, has declared victory over Rep. Lauren Boebert in Colorado’s 4th District, the state’s most conservative seat. 
 CNN has projected her the winner, though the Associated Press has yet to call the race, and Boebert’s campaign has said it is preparing for a recount.
 The coalition kept its leadership team. Gluesenkamp Perez will continue to chair the coalition, and Rep. Adam Gray, D-Calif., will stay on as chair of the Blue Dog PAC.
 Gray knows something about winning on hard ground. A Merced native, he served a decade in the California State Assembly before winning California’s 13th Congressional District in 2024 by just 187 votes, the closest House race in the country that year. He won reelection this month.
 “This election showed that Democrats can win in places where we’ve struggled for years when we listen to voters, respect their communities, and focus on the issues that matter in their daily lives,” Gray said in a statement.
 “Our new members come from different parts of the country, but they share a common understanding that our job is to represent the people who sent us here, not the loudest voices in Washington,” he continued.
 The PAC said it raised a record $3 million for its members this cycle. Federal filings reviewed by Drop Site before the election showed the PAC had raised about $2.2 million to that point. Blue Dog Action, the coalition’s separate super PAC, had raised more than $7.2 million.
 The coalition is also adding incumbents. On Wednesday it welcomed Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet of Michigan’s 8th District, a first-term Democrat who represents a district President Donald Trump carried.
 “I’m proud to join the Blue Dog Coalition, a group of solid, down-to-earth members who understand the concerns of everyday people because they come from those same communities,” McDonald Rivet said.
 The coalition said it was “thrilled to welcome her into our ranks as we reclaim gavels and get to work.” 
 One centrist-focused newsletter wrote that more incumbents may be headed for what it called a “suddenly popular centrist faction.”
 A Center-Left Majority, and a Restless Left 
 The Blue Dogs are not the only moderates growing. On Tuesday, the New Democrat Coalition unanimously admitted 40 members-elect, the largest freshman class in its 30-year history. 
 That brings it to a record 142 members, which the group says is more than half of the incoming Democratic Caucus. 
 The coalition then elected Rep. Nikki Budzinski, D-Ill., to succeed Rep. Brad Schneider, D-Ill., as chair.
 “Imagine a tent, a big tent. It’s all but impossible to raise the tent from the edges. But, if you lift from the center, and you lift high, you can raise the tent and have room for everyone,” Schneider said. 
 He noted that the coalition had 43 members when he arrived in Congress in 2012.
 The two centrist groups overlap heavily. At least nine of the New Dems’ 40 incoming members also posed for the Blue Dogs’ class photo this week, according to a comparison of the coalitions’ rosters. Among them are Garcia, Pulido, Mendoza and Ager.
 The growth on the center-right of the caucus sets up a contest over the agenda of the new majority. Progressives have been organizing too.
 Before the election, Politico reported that the Congressional Progressive Caucus had brought incumbent and incoming members to Washington to plan strategy and lay out what Rep. Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., called “non-negotiables.” 
 Likely members of the new liberal cohort, which some have nicknamed “The Bloc,” campaigned on ending U.S. aid to Israel, abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement and passing “Medicare for All.”
 “There’s going to be some real tension, because we have to move,” Ramirez told Politico.
 Moderates say they have been just as busy. “Just like with the progressives, there have been conversations among moderates about our policy priorities, with a clear proactive agenda,” Rep. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J., a longtime leader of the moderate wing and a Blue Dog, told Politico before the election. 
 He said he expected some colleagues on the left to push “policy red lines that are too extreme and out of step with our democratic values.”
 House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to become speaker, has reportedly previewed an early slate of bills. 
 They include rolling back Republican-led Medicaid cuts, restoring expired Affordable Care Act subsidies and ending Trump’s tariffs. Both wings say they have his ear.
 The line between the factions is not always clear. Rep.-elect Brian Poindexter, called a “Bernie Dog” because both the Progressive Caucus and the Blue Dogs endorsed him, is now affiliated with neither group. Two incoming members, Forstag and Brooks, still belong to both.
 An Agenda Already in Motion 
 The coalition’s legislative work began before the election. On Oct. 9, Golden, Gluesenkamp Perez and Gray introduced the Congressional Budget Reform Act of 2026 (H.R. 10780), a package aimed at the national debt and at overhauling how Congress writes its budgets.
 The bill would combine the 12 annual appropriations bills into four larger packages. It would also automatically extend funding in the short term to head off government shutdowns, and keep Congress in session until spending bills are finished.
 Budgets would have to include debt or deficit targets, and the rules against deficit spending would get tougher. The package also includes “fiscal stress tests” to prepare for economic and national security emergencies.
 The bill will expire with the current Congress in January, but it gives the expanded coalition a ready-made agenda to bring back once Democrats hold the gavels.
 The Blue Dogs have also endorsed the Senate-negotiated Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, a permitting reform bill, as well as a manager’s amendment to it.
 Earlier this year, the coalition said it secured provisions in the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, a sweeping housing package that became law on July 11. 
 Among them are rural housing reforms, small-dollar mortgage provisions and steps to cut regulatory barriers to building. And during National Police Week in May, the Blue Dogs endorsed a slate of law enforcement and first-responder bills, including the Protect and Serve Act, the HELPER Act and the Invest to Protect Act.
 Questions About Spending 
 The coalition’s success has not entirely settled questions about its campaign choices.
 Drop Site reported that Blue Dog Action’s largest expenditure after the primaries, $1.73 million, went to protecting Rep. Mike Thompson, D-Calif., the Blue Dog PAC’s treasurer. 
 Thompson was in a general election against another Democrat, Eric Jones, a former venture capitalist who largely funded his own campaign.
 Thompson, who has served in Congress since 1999, posed with the coalition for its class photo this week. He now appears to have lost. 
 On Thursday, Decision Desk HQ projected Jones the winner, with Jones leading by more than 4 percentage points. The Associated Press has not yet called the race.
 The super PAC spent $700,000 in the primary to help Bale Dalton, a retired Navy captain and former NASA chief of staff, win the Democratic nomination in Florida’s 7th District. In the general election, Drop Site reported, the money went to Thompson instead. 
 Dalton came close. Republican Ryan Elijah won the seat, 49.71% to 49.21%, a margin of about 1,600 votes.
 Phil Gardner, a co-founder of the Blue Dogs’ super PAC and a senior adviser to Gluesenkamp Perez, had criticized the House Majority PAC in an interview with Axios. 
 HMP had cut its ad reservations in the Florida race from $3.9 million to $1.95 million while spending heavily in Maine. Gardner called Dalton “one of the party’s best recruits.” HMP later added $1.7 million in Florida.
 Before the election, a Democratic member of Congress, speaking to Drop Site on condition of anonymity, argued that “money has to be moved to the races that are in most need, regardless of what flavor of Democrat they are.”
 Gardner rejected the criticism in comments to Drop Site. He said the group had discussed its investments with HMP’s leadership in advance, and that the super PAC had sent HMP $225,000 in the two weeks before the election.
 “I’m confident on the whole this cycle Blue Dog Action has more than done its part to support House Democrats in their work to win the majority,” Gardner told Drop Site.
 “We have an opportunity to build a broader, stronger Democratic Party that competes everywhere,” Gray said in announcing his return as PAC chair, “puts people ahead of partisan politics, and stays focused on lowering costs and making life better for American families.”
